Across 12 evals (66 iterations, no run failures), 2 evals ("non-llm-outage-must-not-trigger" and "workload-not-identified-no-premature-binding") were should_trigger:false cases and were fully skipped for expected-output, assertions, and comparisons — both variants correctly did not fire in those cases (trigger_fired 3/3 for both), so these contribute no differentiating data.

For the remaining 10 evals, the trigger fired 3/3 for both variants in every case, so triggering behavior itself is not a point of difference.

**Expected-output match:** This is where the two variants diverge most. Variant_a met the expected output at 100% or 67% in most evals (e.g. transient-vs-config-verdict 3/3, incident-signature-match 3/3, inv-dependency-failure 3/3, third-party-model-boundary-disclosed 3/3, inv-no-evidence-counterfactual 3/3, fa-healthy-agent-status 3/3), while without_skill matched expected output notably less often in several of these same evals — most starkly 0/3 on transient-vs-config-verdict, telemetry-readiness-gap, and agent-loop-on-lambda-binding, and 1/3 on self-hosted-model-locus-not-provider and inv-dependency-failure. In a couple of evals (self-hosted-model-locus-not-provider, inv-cross-region-latency) without_skill matched expected output less or more often than with_skill with mixed assertion results, and in incident-signature-match, third-party-model-boundary-disclosed, inv-no-evidence-counterfactual, and fa-healthy-agent-status, the two were tied or close on expected-output match. Confidence on these judgments is generally high-to-medium, though a few (e.g. telemetry-readiness-gap for with_skill) rest on medium confidence.

**Per-assertion detail:** Several assertions passed for both variants consistently (e.g. "structured ruling" in transient-vs-config-verdict, several always_passes items in incident-signature-match, third-party-model-boundary-disclosed, inv-no-evidence-counterfactual) — these aren't differentiating. A few assertions failed for both variants regardless of variant, notably the catalog check-id regex assertions in transient-vs-config-verdict and inv-cross-region-latency (always_fails), suggesting that specific behavior/assertion needs work rather than reflecting a variant difference. Several assertions showed a clear split favoring with_skill (e.g. "states what it observed for each signal," "identifies specific missing telemetry," "names the hosting binding," "addresses graceful degradation/isolation of the dependency" all with_skill_passes_without_skill_fails), with no assertions in the data showing the reverse clean pattern (without_skill passing while with_skill fails outright), though some "flaky" assertions (inconsistent across runs) show without_skill underperforming with_skill by one or two runs (e.g. locus classification in self-hosted-model-locus-not-provider actually favored without_skill 3/3 vs with_skill 2/3).

**Quality comparisons (pairwise):** Mixed and eval-dependent, with many pairs skipped (comparisons marked skipped in 4 of the 10 active evals, reducing confidence in some of these). Where quality pairs were evaluated, with_skill was favored more in incident-signature-match (6 vs 4), inv-dependency-failure (2 vs 0), and inv-no-evidence-counterfactual (8 vs 1), while without_skill was favored more in self-hosted-model-locus-not-provider (1 vs 0, only 1 pair evaluated), third-party-model-boundary-disclosed (6 vs 3), inv-cross-region-latency (4 vs 2), and fa-healthy-agent-status (6 vs 3). Confidence on these quality judgments is generally medium.

**Runtime and cost:** Variant_a consistently took longer and cost more per run across almost every eval (e.g. 1m53s/$0.94 vs 3m27s/$1.72 is a case where without_skill was slower — but in most other evals the opposite held, with with_skill running longer, e.g. 1m29s/$0.74 vs 39s/$0.33 in telemetry-readiness-gap, 1m34s/$0.78 vs 27s/$0.23 in agent-loop-on-lambda-binding, 36s/$0.30 vs 0s/$0.00 in self-hosted-model-locus-not-provider). In a few cases (transient-vs-config-verdict, self-hosted-model-locus-not-provider, inv-dependency-failure) without_skill's runtime/cost registered as 0s/$0.00, which likely reflects early/trivial responses rather than a true zero-cost run, and coincides with those being evals where without_skill also scored lowest on expected-output match. Runtime-threshold exceedances were rare except in inv-no-evidence-counterfactual, where with_skill exceeded the 30s threshold in all 3 pairs.

**Output consistency (run-to-run stability):** Mixed, with no systematic advantage either way. Variant_a was flagged "inconsistent" in telemetry-readiness-gap and incident-signature-match, while without_skill was flagged "inconsistent" in agent-loop-on-lambda-binding; most other evals rated both as "mostly_consistent" or "consistent" with no large gap.

**Overall pattern:** Variant_a tended to meet the expected output and pass individual assertions more often across a majority of the active evals, often also running longer and costing more, while without_skill was sometimes faster/cheaper but missed expected output entirely in several evals (notably zero matches in 3 of 10 active evals) and underperformed on a handful of binding/signal-reporting assertions. Pairwise quality judgments were more evenly split across evals, sometimes favoring without_skill even in cases where it missed the strict expected-output match, and several key assertions (e.g. catalog check-id) failed for both variants, indicating a shared gap rather than a between-variant difference. Given the mix of skipped comparisons, medium-confidence quality judgments, and flaky/variable per-run results in several assertions, this picture reflects real but uneven differences rather than a uniform advantage for either variant.

transient-vs-config-verdict.summary:

Assertions (18 total, aggregated across runs): with_skill passed 13/18 (72%), without_skill passed 8/18 (44%). Breaking this down by individual assertion:
- Two assertions passed for both variants at 100% ("presents classification as a structured ruling" and "if PROVIDER locus, prescribes no customer config change") — these aren't differentiating since both systems handle them equally well.
- One assertion ("at least one finding carries a catalog check-id") failed for both variants at 0% — this suggests either the assertion or the underlying behavior needs attention regardless of variant.
- One assertion ("names an explicit locus") was flaky for without_skill (2/3) vs consistent for with_skill (3/3).
- One assertion ("reports server-error rate across multiple models") was weak for both: with_skill only 1/3, without_skill 0/3 — neither variant reliably satisfies this, with with_skill only marginally ahead.
- One assertion ("states what it actually observed for each signal, including explicitly noting no-data") showed a clear split: with_skill passed 3/3 while without_skill failed 0/3 (without_skill's confidence here was medium, slightly lower than its other high-confidence results). This is the most notable single-assertion difference and aligns with the expected-output gap.

Metrics: with_skill averaged 29s runtime and $0.25 cost per run, with 5.1% context utilization and no compactions. without_skill averaged 0s runtime and $0.00 cost, with 4.2% context utilization and no compactions. This is a substantial resource/time difference, but it accompanies the quality/correctness gap above — without_skill's near-zero runtime and cost may reflect a much lighter or incomplete process rather than simply being more efficient, given it failed to meet expected output in any run.

Quality comparison: no paired quality comparisons could be completed (0 pairs evaluated, 3 skipped), so there is no direct head-to-head quality judgment available for this dimension.

Output consistency: with_skill was rated "mostly_consistent" (score 2.0/3, high confidence), while without_skill was rated fully "consistent" (score 3.0/3, high confidence). So without_skill produced more uniform outputs run-to-run, even though those consistent outputs failed to meet the expected output and underperformed on several assertions.

Overall, the picture is mixed but leans toward a tradeoff: with_skill met the expected output and several key assertions (notably explicit observation-reporting) much more reliably, at the cost of higher runtime and spend, while without_skill was cheaper, faster, and more internally consistent, but that consistency corresponded to consistently not meeting the expected output and weaker performance on several assertions. One assertion (catalog check-id) failed for both, indicating a shared gap unrelated to the variant difference. All findings here are based on a small sample (3 runs per variant) and no comparative quality-pair data was available.
